analysis.body:
The Census BTOS measure for professional, scientific, and technical services (NAICS 54, which includes legal) puts AI use at 43.3% in the latest period, up from 41.9% in the prior period. The question asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and it was first asked in September 2023. Because the NAICS category covers the broader professional services sector, this is not a legal-only figure, but it is the closest official adoption number available for the industry.

What legal AI is deployed for is well documented across the sources. Per Legaltech Hub, OpenAI's Astra for Law is a model configuration built initially for Am Law 200 firms that pairs the GPT-6 Astra model with legal knowledge, tools, and ecosystem plugins. Legaltech Hub also describes Transcript Genius, a Steno deposition transcript analysis tool that mines deposition and trial transcripts for summaries, data points, and strategic insights, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document and pleading verification. The same source notes that generative AI is taking over document review, first drafts, and due diligence. Per ILTA, Epiq has released Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access, while Litify has expanded ACE with firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity. Stanford CodeX runs programs for agentic AI applications at the intersection of technology and law and builds computational models of legal systems.

The vendor and model landscape is catalogued in two places. The legal models catalog on this site tracks the 1,000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads, and release date refreshed daily, all tuned for legal text. Legaltech Hub positions itself as a global directory where buyers can research legal technology, vendors can showcase solutions, and investors can understand the marketplace. The sources do not report dollar figures for spending or returns, but the vendor activity they describe concentrates in document review, deposition analysis, legal research, contract review, workflow automation, and agentic reasoning.

On risk and regulation, the ABA is the profession's reference point. Per the ABA, its Center for Innovation continues to address the impact of AI on the legal profession, including ethical considerations, and provides guidance on trustworthy and responsible development and use of AI, with strategies to mitigate AI-related risks. The ABA's sourced point identifies Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI ethics as the profession's reference point. Stanford CodeX runs an international conference uniting legal experts, policymakers, and business leaders to harness AI for sustainable, ethical, and responsible legal systems. The legal models catalog on this site also tracks state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, and compliance frameworks. One risk the sources flag is not financial: Legaltech Hub reports that as generative AI takes over document review, first drafts, and due diligence, firms are confronting the loss of junior lawyer training, because those repetitive tasks were where lawyers developed judgment, and firms are experimenting with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those learning opportunities.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the sources point to independent evaluation and professional guidance as the main checks. Vals AI benchmarks legal reasoning on legal research, case-law synthesis, and statutory interpretation, described as the vendor-neutral test of whether legal AI actually reasons. The ABA's guidance on risk management, governance, and generative AI ethics is the profession's reference point. Adoption in the broader professional services category is rising, and the tooling is mature enough to cover research, drafting, review, and deposition analysis, but the sources do not provide ROI figures, and the training pipeline effect on junior lawyers is an open concern that efficiency metrics do not capture.

https://www.iltanet.org/.brief: ILTA, which calls itself a trusted global resource community for legal technologists, observes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs and that its Spring Peer to Peer topics reflect this evolution. Epiq announced the availability of Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access. Litify says its ACE product now offers firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity for legal teams.

https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/.brief: Legaltech Hub presents itself as a worldwide catalogue of legal technology products and services, aimed at buyers, vendors, and investors. The page notes that OpenAI has released Astra for Law, a configuration of its GPT-6 Astra model tailored for legal work and initially built for Am Law 200 firms. It also highlights Steno’s Transcript Genius, an AI tool for analyzing deposition and trial transcripts, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, summarization, contract review, and document verification. A further item examines how generative AI automating document review and first drafts may remove learning opportunities for junior lawyers, and describes firm experiments with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those opportunities.

https://law.stanford.edu/codex-the-stanf.brief: CodeX is a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science that studies how information technology can improve legal processes. It applies data science and artificial intelligence to build quantitative and predictive models of the law, moving beyond traditional empirical analysis. The program offers a hands-on accelerated track for interdisciplinary student teams to prototype Agentic AI and the CFAA applications at the intersection of technology and law. CodeX also hosts a hackathon that brings together AI innovators, machine learning specialists, and legal professionals to prototype future legal technology. Additionally, it organizes an international conference and FutureLaw 2026 to bring together leaders in law, technology, and policy to discuss sustainable, ethical, and responsible AI in legal systems.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page reports that it catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model’s licence, download count, and release date. According to the page, the list is refreshed daily and is built from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page also states that its full-text search covers other resources built from the same database, including state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, and a glossary.

https://www.americanbar.org/groups/cente.brief: The Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has finished its work, and the Center for Innovation will keep addressing how AI affects the legal profession, including ethical issues, trustworthy development, and risk-mitigation strategies. It will also provide guidance on responsible AI use. Past webinars from the Task Force examine how AI is reshaping law practice, covering practical applications, new legal technology, and the ethical, professional-responsibility, and regulatory challenges lawyers must navigate.
